record.program_name: Permanent Local Housing Allocation (PLHA), County formula allocation
record.administering_agency: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency, Neighborhood Preservation Division

record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). record.program_name: Affordable Housing Density Bonus, Development Title Chapter 9-401 (unincorporated county)
record.administering_agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department
record.typical_award_size: State-law density bonus codified in Chapter 9-401 (2026-10 code edition): 20% base bonus for 10% low-income, 5% very low-income or senior projects; 5% for 10% moderate-income for-sale units; 20% for 10% very low-income units for veterans, transition-age youth or homeless households; 35% for qualifying student housing; sliding scale up to 50% (2.5% per 1% very low-income above 5%, 1.5% per 1% low-income above 10%); land donation bonus 15% to 35%; floor area ratio bonus in the R-H zone for infill near transit with 20% of units at or below 50% AMI; 100% lower-income projects per Government Code 65915. One to four incentives or concessions by affordability tier plus parking reductions; the County may exceed these amounts (9-401.060).
record.per_unit_cap: Not applicable.
record.affordability_requirement: 55-year rental affordability (longer if required by financing); for-sale units sold to qualifying buyers with equity sharing; affordable units integrated with and indistinguishable from market-rate units; replacement of existing affordable units required.
record.next_deadline: By application; pre-application response within 90 days; streamlined ministerial approval under 9-401.120 for eligible infill projects with at least 10% of units at or below 80% AMI (60 or 90 day review, deemed approved if missed).
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). The unincorporated county has no inclusionary ordinance and no in-lieu fee, so the density bonus and concessions are the only land-use subsidy; the 2023-2031 Housing Element (HCD submittal revised January 2025, adopted and revised June 30, 2026 to transfer RHNA to the new City of Mountain House, 8,808 to 5,113 units) sets a quantified objective of 100 lower-income units through the bonus and commits to fee deferrals for affordable subdivisions. The ministerial pathway in 9-401.120 carries state prevailing wage and skilled workforce requirements for larger projects under Government Code 65913.4, so model labor costs before electing it. Most multifamily sites in the unincorporated county (French Camp, Garden Acres, Lodi and Stockton fringe) are constrained by water and sewer service, which the Housing Element names as the largest constraint. Source is the published Development Title chapter on gocodebook.com (County code host); confirm current text with Community Development at (209) 468-3144.

HCD-hosted Housing Element was the only agency document that could be opened; slocity.org (403) and the City eScribe agenda host pub-slocity.escribemeetings.com (filestream 403, JS-only listings) could not be read, so current fund balance and 2025-2026 awards are unconfirmed.
record.audit_note: Core program facts (Program 2.5, Res. 9263 criteria, grant and below-market loan use, ELI through moderate income, 55/45 year terms, $10.45M history) confirmed in the HCD-hosted Housing Element; post-2020 award figures could not be confirmed because slocity.org returns 403.

record.program_name: Development services fee waiver and citywide development impact fee deferral loans for affordable units (Housing Element incentives table; Chapter 4.56 impact fee deferral)
record.administering_agency: City of San Luis Obispo Community Development Department and Finance Department
record.typical_award_size: Residential projects meeting City affordable housing standards for extremely low, very low and low income households are exempt from all planning, engineering and building review, processing and permit fees and water and sewer meter hook-up fees; mixed-income projects receive the waiver per affordable unit. Citywide development impact fees are deferred (as a deferral loan) for affordable units that exceed the inclusionary minimum or are built, owned and managed by HASLO, other public agencies or nonprofit housing agencies. Example: Bishop Street Studios received an impact fee deferral loan as part of $1,595,500 in City assistance; 2023 HASLO awards for 736 Orcutt and 279 Bridge Street each included a fee deferral loan. HCD's Prohousing release describes the impact fee relief as a waiver for qualifying affordable housing.
record.affordability_requirement: Deed-restricted affordable units at City Affordable Housing Standards (extremely low, very low, low for the fee exemption; any inclusionary-exceeding or nonprofit or public agency affordable unit for impact fee deferral).
record.next_deadline: Not applicable; requested with the building permit or through the AHF award resolution.
record.layering_notes: Local cost-reduction layer that stacks with AHF awards; the City routinely packages an AHF loan plus an impact fee deferral loan in one resolution. Fee exemptions and deferrals are public subsidies and may trigger Labor Code 1720 prevailing wage unless the project already pays it under LIHTC or state funding. The Chapter 4.56 ordinance text and current deferral terms (interest, repayment at permanent loan closing versus residual receipts) could not be opened because slocity.org, codepublishing and the City eScribe agenda host all block automated access; the HCD-hosted 2020 Housing Element incentives table is the source. No comparable county program exists for unincorporated land beyond the Title 22 incentive program.

record.program_name: Affordable housing fee deferral loans (deferral of development impact, water and sewer connection and building permit fees; Housing Element Programs 8 and 9)
record.administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department and City Council (case-by-case resolution)
record.typical_award_size: Case-by-case Council approval of long-term deferral of City water connection, sewer connection, development impact and building permit fees, structured as General Fund loans repaid several years beyond occupancy. Oak Park Public Housing (Paso Robles Housing Authority) phases one through four received fee deferral loans of $1.018 million (Resolution 12-031), $889,000 (14-019), $999,423 (17-019) and $1,438,160.71 (Resolution 18-020, 2018). Resolution 18-020 terms: promissory note repaid over up to 30 years from building permit at 3.75% simple interest from residual receipts, secured by a deed of trust. News reports (not agency sources) describe a March 2026 Council resolution deferring water, sewer, development impact and building permit fees for affordable housing, a 30-year deferral of about $1.2 million for Highland's Senior Affordable Apartments (298 Niblick Road), a 30-year deferral of about $1.8 million for Sunrise Villas Apartments, a roughly 50% impact fee waiver for a nine-unit Habitat for Humanity project on Vine Street, and February 2021 deferrals for a 79-unit senior project at Woodland Plaza II.
record.affordability_requirement: Units affordable to lower-income households (Health and Safety Code 50079.5), including extremely low income; City practice requires a recorded affordability covenant for the longest feasible time and not less than 30 years (Resolution 18-020).
record.next_deadline: Rolling; no open round or deadline as of November 8, 2026. Requests go to Council with the entitlement or before building permit; contact Community Development at (805) 237-3970 or planning@prcity.com.
record.layering_notes: This is the only City-controlled financial tool in Paso Robles; it substitutes for a housing trust fund. City fee deferrals have been the local match for Paso Robles Housing Authority tax credit deals (Oak Park) and are expected to pair with County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund awards, HASLO or Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund loans and the Urban County HOME NOFA (county record). The City receives about $165,000 per year of CDBG through the Urban County, which cannot fund new construction or impact fees. The 2026 resolution and project-specific deferrals were found only in local news; the City's eScribe agenda host (pub-pasorobles.escribemeetings.com) renders listings in JavaScript and returns 403 on document downloads, so the HCD-hosted 2020-2028 Housing Element is the agency source. Paso Robles is now preparing its 7th cycle Housing Element (consultant RFP due September 8, 2026).
record.cycle_notes: No NOFA. Housing Element Program 7 (Affordable Housing Support) commits the City to offer impact fee deferrals for lower-income units and allow deferral of fees several years beyond occupancy; each deferral is approved by Council resolution.
record.audit_note: Program number corrected to Housing Element Program 7 (Programs 8 and 9 are Uptown/Town Centre and Homelessness). Past February 12, 2026 committee date removed from next_deadline. 2026 project deferrals remain news-sourced.

record.program_name: Inclusionary housing ordinance and local affordable housing fund (none adopted; Housing Element finding)
record.administering_agency: City of El Paso de Robles Community Development Department, Housing Programs Division
record.typical_award_size: None. The 2020-2028 Housing Element states the City of Paso Robles does not have an inclusionary ordinance, and the City holds no inclusionary in-lieu fund, local housing trust fund or RDA successor housing fund for development. The Housing Programs Division's development support is limited to CDBG (about $165,000 per year through the Urban County), applying for County-administered HOME funds, fee deferrals and liaison with the Paso Robles Housing Authority. A November 2025 townhouse proposal offered a voluntary in-lieu payment tied to the County's Title 22 point system for use in a future tax-credit project, which indicates ad hoc negotiated contributions rather than a program.
record.affordability_requirement: Not applicable.
record.next_deadline: Not applicable; no program exists as of November 8, 2026. Watch the 7th cycle Housing Element update for any inclusionary or local housing fund program.
record.layering_notes: Negative finding recorded so the gap is visible: Paso Robles is the largest North County city and offers no local gap funding beyond fee deferrals. Developers must rely on County Title 29 and the new Regional Housing Fund (county records), HASLO and Paso Robles Housing Authority vouchers, SLO County Housing Trust Fund and state programs. The 2020 Housing Element workshops listed a possible local housing fund (General Fund, TOT, in-lieu fees) as an option but none was adopted. prcity.com pages and the HCD-hosted Housing Element were opened; the 2025 Annual Progress Report could not be located on prcity.com.
record.audit_note: Kept funding_type other: this is a negative finding with no deployable fund; the Housing Element states the City has no inclusionary ordinance and lists only General Fund fee deferral loans, Urban County CDBG and HOME, and the private SLO County Housing Trust Fund as resources.

record.program_name: Affordable Housing Impact Fee Deferral Program (Municipal Code Section 3-14.070 as amended by Ord. 666, September 26, 2023, and Council deferral resolution)
record.administering_agency: City of Atascadero Community Development Department and Administrative Services
record.typical_award_size: Development impact fees and wastewater capacity charges, normally due at final inspection, may be deferred under a Council-approved agreement for residential units affordable to low, very low or extremely low income households. Staff reports and local coverage describe the program as a 17-year interest-bearing deferral loan for projects with five or more affordable rental units, with up to about $3 million in fees eligible; the City cites multifamily impact fees of roughly $12,000 to $15,000 per unit. Intended to improve TCAC competitiveness by lowering upfront cost.
record.per_unit_cap: About $12,000 to $15,000 per high-density multifamily unit in impact fees is deferrable, not waived.
record.affordability_requirement: Units affordable to low, very low and extremely low income households under a recorded agreement; deferral terms set in the agreement approved by Council.
record.next_deadline: Not applicable; request with the entitlement or before building permit issuance. Contact Community Development at (805) 461-5000.
record.layering_notes: Deferral, not forgiveness: fees are a City loan repaid over the term, so underwrite as soft debt. Implements Housing Element Program 2.E. EPS advised the City against outright impact fee waivers for fiscal reasons, so a waiver is unlikely. Stacks with state density bonus (Article 30), the inclusionary in-lieu fund, County Title 29 or Regional Housing Fund, HASLO vouchers and Urban County HOME. The ordinance text was read on the ecode360 code mirror (atascadero.org links to the September 26, 2023 resolution on records.atascadero.org, which returned a scanned PDF with no extractable text).

record.program_name: Inclusionary Affordable Housing Trust Fund (In-Lieu Affordable Housing Fund) grants to affordable developments (Housing Element Program C.1-1)
